events.credibility_reason: Several F10 signals together: a landmark claim with no expert uptake in ~21 months; independent author outside the field; 14 revisions with title and framing changing and file size swinging 43KB->885KB->29KB; later 2026 papers by working combinatorialists still call the conjecture open and do not cite it; reported omitted proofs (Remark 2.1).
The author withdrew the arXiv paper (v4, 23 Jul 2026). The order-at-most-7 check is in any case only instances already implied by Kaneko-Locke; the split-twin families are the case content.
Withdrawn by the author, with a comment saying counterexamples were found; the content concerns the paper's own Pisa-graph conjecture, and no counterexample to Seymour's conjecture is described.

events.ai_basis: OpenAI language models (GPT-5 family) carried out the detailed mathematical exploration, implemented counterexample searches and verification tools, discovered the fixed-target capacity argument and its double-counting proof, and drafted the manuscript;

events.ai_basis: The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model.

why: The OpenAI manuscript's Theorem 1.1 is stated for every nonempty finite oriented graph, which matches the statement word for word, so its scope is whole. It is only 8 days old, and the only check is a Lean build whose sorry-free status is not recorded (F7), so it is unreviewed. That is not a reason for doubt (F10), so it is credible. The README says the results came from an unreleased internal OpenAI model, so it is generated. Glover's claim is also whole in scope, but it has several F10 signals at once: an independent author, 14 revisions with the title and framing changing, no uptake in about 21 months, and later papers by specialists that still call the problem open. So it is not_credible. Brukhman's AI credit says the model discovered the key argument and its proof, which makes it generated. Sadhukhan et al.'s credit says ChatGPT helped develop the CP-SAT encodings, which are verification code that the authors then ran and audited themselves. Under F12 that is none, but it is a close call. Halkiewicz's paper was withdrawn by its author, so both of its rows are knocked_down. Espuny Diaz et al. is an 'almost every graph' statement about a random model rather than a class of graphs, so I scored it as bound (a proportion) and not as case. Bai, Li and Park prove a stronger matching form, and its only new territory for the original question is planar and 5-anti-transitive graphs, so I scored it as a variant. The Liu et al. date cannot be placed.
doubts: There are two close calls. (1) Sadhukhan et al.: the AI-developed CP-SAT encodings carry the finite cases of the proof, so 'assisted' is a defensible alternative to 'none'. The quote only says 'with assistance', and I judged that too thin. (2) The OpenAI attribution rests on a README sentence covering the 'vast majority' of results, not one specific to this manuscript. The Lean scope text matches the statement, but sorry_free is null. The result has not been independently verified, and its correctness is untested after 8 days. Liu et al.'s actual result was never read, so its scope as a case rests on the title alone.
